'''Margaret Jean McFall-Ngai''' (born 1951) is an American animal physiologist and biochemist<ref name="Future Tech Podcast" /> best-known for her work related to the symbiotic relationship between Hawaiian [[bobtail squid]], ''[[Euprymna scolopes]]'' and [[bioluminescent bacteria]], ''[[Vibrio fischeri]]''. Her research helped expand the microbiology field, primarily focused on [[pathogenicity]] and decomposition at the time, to include positive microbial associations.<ref name = "Yong 2015">{{cite journal |last1=Yong |first1=E |title=Microbiology: Here's looking at you, squid. |journal=Nature |date=15 January 2015 |volume=517 |issue=7534 |pages=262–4 |doi=10.1038/517262a |pmid=25592518|bibcode=2015Natur.517..262Y |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Viegas 2017" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Margaret McFall-Ngai |url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/margaret-mcfall-ngai/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180828102146/https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/margaret-mcfall-ngai/ |archive-date=28 August 2018 |website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation |access-date=2 December 2019}}</ref> She has been a professor at PBRC's Kewalo Marine Laboratory <ref name="McFall-Ngai CV" /> and director of the Pacific Biosciences Research Program at the [[University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa]].<ref name="Pacific Biosciences Research Center 2017" /> In 2022, she joined [[Carnegie Institution for Science|Carnegie Institution for Science's]] newly created Biosphere Sciences & Engineering research division and moved her laboratory to [[Caltech]], in [[Pasadena, California]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Glowing Squid {{!}} Home page |url=https://www.glowingsquid.org/ |access-date=2024-11-27 |website=www.glowingsquid.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-08-27 |title=Dr. Margaret McFall-Ngai |url=https://carnegiescience.edu/bio/dr-margaret-mcfall-ngai-0 |url-status=live |access-date=2026-08-27 |website=Carnegie Science}}</ref>  

==Education and career==
McFall-Ngai spent her childhood in Southern California and attended [[Immaculate Heart High School (Los Angeles)|Immaculate Heart High School]] in Los Angeles.<ref name="Viegas 2017">{{Cite journal|last=Viegas|first=Jennifer|date=2017-08-22|title=Profile of Margaret J. McFall-Ngai|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=114|issue=36|language=en|pages=9494–9496|doi=10.1073/pnas.1713158114|issn=0027-8424|pmid=28830998|pmc=5594705|bibcode=2017PNAS..114.9494V |doi-access=free}}</ref> She attended college at the [[University of San Francisco]], graduating in 1973 with a Bachelors of Science in biology.<ref name="Viegas 2017" /> She chose to further her education at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] (UCLA) with [[doctoral advisor]], James Morin, studying functional morphology and [[comparative physiology]]<ref name = "Amato 2018">{{cite news |last1=Amato |first1=Katherine |title=Q&A With Margaret McFall-Ngai |url=https://www.cifar.ca/cifarnews/2018/07/31/q-a-with-margaret-mcfall-ngai}}</ref> while working as a teaching assistant/fellow.<ref name = "McFall-Ngai CV">{{cite web |last1=McFall-Ngai |first1=Margaret |title=McFall-Ngai CV |url=http://www.kewalo.hawaii.edu/images/faculty/McFallNgai_papers/McFallNgaiCV.pdf |access-date=1 December 2019}}</ref> Her graduate research took her to the central Philippines to study the relationship between bioluminescent bacteria found in the [[leiognathid]] light organ in fish,<ref name = "McFall-Ngai and Dunlap">{{cite journal |last1=McFall-Ngai |first1=Margaret |title=Three new modes of luminescence in the leiognathid fish Gazza minuta: Discrete projected luminescence, ventral body flash, and buccal luminescence |journal=Marine Biology |date=April 1983 |volume=73 |issue=3 |pages=227–237|doi=10.1007/BF00392247 |s2cid=84813290}}</ref><ref name = "McFall-Ngai 1983">{{cite journal |last1=McFall-Ngai |first1=Margaret |title=Adaptations for reflection of bioluminescent light in the gas bladder of Leiognathus equulus (Perciformes: Leiognathidae). |journal=Journal of Experimental Zoology |date=July 1983 |volume=227 |issue=1 |pages=23–33 |doi=10.1002/jez.1402270105 |pmid=6619765}}</ref> igniting her "lifelong interest"<ref name="Viegas 2017" /> in the blend of the two subjects. McFall-Ngai graduated with her Ph.D. in Biology in 1983 and went on to complete two postdoctoral fellowships.<ref name = "Pacific Biosciences Research Center 2017">{{cite web |last1=McFall-Ngai |first1=Margaret |title=Margaret McFall-Ngai, PH.D |url=http://www.pbrc.hawaii.edu/index.php/margaret-mcfall-ngai |website=Pacific Biosciences Research Center |publisher=Pacific Biosciences Research Center, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa |access-date=1 December 2019}}</ref> For her first postdoc, she remained at UCLA working on [[protein]] biochemistry-biophysics<ref name="Amato 2018" /> for the [[Jules Stein Eye Institute]] with advisor, Joseph Horwitz.<ref name="McFall-Ngai CV" /> She then moved to San Diego to work with advisor George Somero on protein chemistry enzymology<ref name="Amato 2018" /> at the [[Scripps Institute of Oceanography]] at the [[University of California, San Diego]].<ref name="McFall-Ngai CV" /> On the side McFall-Ngai had been exploring the Hawaiian bobtail squid as an alternative to the fish she had studied in graduate school and initiated what would become a career-long collaboration with [[microbiologist]], [[Edward G. Ruby|Edward (Ned) Ruby]], who had written his dissertation on the squids' symbionts, ''[[Vibrio fischeri]]''.<ref name = "Future Tech Podcast">{{cite web |title=Hawaiian Bobtail Squid: Using Light to Hide in the Dark—Dr. Margaret Mc-Fall Ngai—The Squid Vibrio Labs |url=https://www.futuretechpodcast.com/podcasts/hawaiian-bobtail-squid-using-light-to-hide-in-the-dark-dr-margaret-mc-fall-ngai-the-squid-vibrio-labs/ |website=FutureTech Podcast |access-date=1 December 2019|date=2019-09-23}}</ref>

In 1989, McFall-Ngai accepted a position and later received tenure at the [[University of Southern California]] in the Department of Biology and began breeding and studying the Hawaiian bobtail squid.<ref name="Yong 2015" /> She and Ruby moved to Hawaii in 1996 to better study the squid-bacteria relationship, both accepting positions at Pacific Biomedical Research Center at the University of Hawaii.<ref name="Pacific Biosciences Research Center 2017" /> In 2004, McFall-Ngai accepted a position as professor in the Department of Medical Microbiology and Immunology at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] and the Eye Research institute.<ref name="U.W-M Bio">{{cite web |title=Margaret J. McFall-Ngai, PH.D |url=https://vision.wisc.edu/staff/mcfall-ngai-phd-margaret-j/ |website=McPherson Eye Research Institute |date=10 August 2017 |access-date=2 December 2019}}</ref> She returned to Hawaii in 2015 when she accepted the position as director of the Pacific Biosciences Research Program<ref name="Pacific Biosciences Research Center 2017" /> and professor at PBRC's Kewalo Marine Laboratory at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa.<ref name="McFall-Ngai CV" />

==Research==
McFall-Ngai is a pioneer in the study of animal-bacterial symbiosis and known for her research of the Hawaiian bobtail squid, ''[[Euprymna scolopes]]'', and its relationship with bacteria, ''[[Vibrio fischeri]]''. She initially began her research in graduate school studying fish with a similar bioluminescent bacterial relationship,<ref name="McFall-Ngai and Dunlap" /><ref name="McFall-Ngai 1983" /> however, these fish proved difficult to grow in the lab. At a meeting, a visiting researcher from the University of Hawaii suggested she investigate the Hawaiian bobtail squid and its bioluminescent symbionts ''V. fischeri'' as an alternative.<ref name="Future Tech Podcast" /> McFall-Ngai found that the squid worked great in the lab with 8-10 pairs of squid generating roughly 60,000 juveniles a year.<ref name="Yong 2015" /> To fully study this relationship, McFall-Ngai began collaborating with Edward (Ned) Ruby, a microbiologist who had written his dissertation on ''V. fischeri''.<ref name="Future Tech Podcast" />

Over the next three decades, McFall-Ngai, Ruby, and dozens of postdocs and students would investigate all aspects of the symbiotic relationship.<ref name="McFall-Ngai - Divining the essence">{{cite journal |last1=McFall-Ngai |first1=M |title=Divining the essence of symbiosis: insights from the squid-vibrio model. |journal=PLOS Biology |date=February 2014 |volume=12 |issue=2 |article-number=e1001783 |doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.1001783 |pmid=24504482|pmc=3913551 |doi-access=free }}</ref> They worked to understand the development of the relationship at different stages of the squid life cycle,<ref name="Montgomery & McFall 1993">{{cite journal |last1=Montgomery |first1=MK |last2=McFall-Ngai |first2=M |title=Embryonic Development of the Light Organ of the Sepiolid Squid Euprymna scolopes Berry. |journal=The Biological Bulletin |date=June 1993 |volume=184 |issue=3 |pages=296–308 |doi=10.2307/1542448 |pmid=29300543|jstor=1542448 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/part/37221}}</ref><ref name="Montgomery McFall 1994">{{cite journal |last1=Montgomery |first1=MK |last2=McFall-Ngai |first2=M |title=Bacterial symbionts induce host organ morphogenesis during early postembryonic development of the squid Euprymna scolopes. |journal=Development |date=July 1994 |volume=120 |issue=7 |pages=1719–29 |doi=10.1242/dev.120.7.1719 |pmid=7924980}}</ref> analyze the initiation of symbiosis in real time,<ref name="Nyholm, Stabb, Ruby, McFall 2000">{{cite journal |last1=Nyholm |first1=SV |last2=Stabb |first2=EV |last3=Ruby |first3=EG |last4=McFall-Ngai |first4=MJ |title=Establishment of an animal-bacterial association: recruiting symbiotic vibrios from the environment. |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |date=29 August 2000 |volume=97 |issue=18 |pages=10231–5 |doi=10.1073/pnas.97.18.10231 |pmid=10963683|pmc=27829 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Foster, McFall 1998">{{cite journal |last1=Foster |first1=JS |last2=McFall-Ngai |first2=MJ |title=Induction of apoptosis by cooperative bacteria in the morphogenesis of host epithelial tissues. |journal=Development Genes and Evolution |date=August 1998 |volume=208 |issue=6 |pages=295–303 |doi=10.1007/s004270050185 |pmid=9716720|s2cid=24818919}}</ref> and identify how the host selects its symbionts.<ref name="Altura, Heath-Heckman, Gilette,etc. 2013">{{cite journal |last1=Altura |first1=MA |last2=Heath-Heckman |first2=EA |last3=Gillette |first3=A |last4=Kremer |first4=N |last5=Krachler |first5=AM |last6=Brennan |first6=C |last7=Ruby |first7=EG |last8=Orth |first8=K |last9=McFall-Ngai |first9=MJ |title=The first engagement of partners in the Euprymna scolopes-Vibrio fischeri symbiosis is a two-step process initiated by a few environmental symbiont cells. |journal=Environmental Microbiology |date=November 2013 |volume=15 |issue=11 |pages=2937–50 |doi=10.1111/1462-2920.12179 |pmid=23819708|pmc=3937295}}</ref><ref name="Visick 2009">{{cite journal |last1=Visick |first1=KL |title=An intricate network of regulators controls biofilm formation and colonization by Vibrio fischeri. |journal=Molecular Microbiology |date=November 2009 |volume=74 |issue=4 |pages=782–9 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2958.2009.06899.x |pmid=19818022|pmc=2906375|author-link=Karen Visick}}</ref><ref name="Wollenberg, Ruby 2009">{{cite journal |last1=Wollenberg |first1=MS |last2=Ruby |first2=EG |title=Population structure of Vibrio fischeri within the light organs of Euprymna scolopes squid from Two Oahu (Hawaii) populations. |journal=Applied and Environmental Microbiology |date=January 2009 |volume=75 |issue=1 |pages=193–202 |doi=10.1128/AEM.01792-08 |pmid=18997024|pmc=2612210|bibcode=2009ApEnM..75..193W }}</ref> They learned that the squid follows a rhythmic pattern in which the bacteria are brightest when the squid hunt at night <ref name="Boettcher, RUby, McFall 1995">{{cite journal |last1=Boettcher |first1=K.J. |last2=Ruby |first2=E.G. |last3=McFall-Ngai |first3=M.J. |title=Bioluminescence in the symbiotic squid Euprymna scolopes is controlled by a daily biological rhythm |journal=Journal of Comparative Physiology A |date=July 1996 |volume=179 |issue=1 |doi=10.1007/BF00193435|s2cid=28096354}}</ref> and are then expelled at dawn.<ref name="Graf, Ruby 1998">{{cite journal |last1=Graf |first1=J |last2=Ruby |first2=EG |title=Host-derived amino acids support the proliferation of symbiotic bacteria. |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |date=17 February 1998 |volume=95 |issue=4 |pages=1818–22 |doi=10.1073/pnas.95.4.1818 |pmid=9465100|pmc=19196 |bibcode=1998PNAS...95.1818G |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Heath-Heckman, etc 2013">{{cite journal |last1=Heath-Heckman |first1=Elizabeth A. |first7=Jo |title=Bacterial Bioluminescence Regulates Expression of a Host Cryptochrome Gene in the Squid-Vibrio Symbiosis |journal=mBio |date=2 April 2013 |volume=4 |issue=2 |first10=E |last11=Almabrazi |first11=H |last12=Scheetz |first12=TE |last13=Bonaldo Mde |first13=F |last14=Casavant |first14=TL |last15=Soares |first15=MB |last16=Cronan |first16=JE |last17=Reed |first17=JL |last18=Ruby |first18=EG |last19=McFall-Ngai |first19=MJ |title=Transcriptional patterns in both host and bacterium underlie a daily rhythm of anatomical and metabolic change in a
